scenes.headline: How a snapshot costs almost nothing
scenes.sub: LayerFS gives each agent a workspace over shared history
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Strata! This is how a filesystem can keep a hundred snapshots without keeping a hundred copies.

scenes.text: A snapshot is a small tree of hashes pointing at chunks that are already stored. Only what changed is written.
scenes.say: A snapshot is just a small tree of hashes, pointing at chunks the store already holds.

scenes.title: From an edit to a commit

steps.say: An agent edits files in its workspace overlay. The chunker cuts files over a hundred and twenty-eight kibibytes where their content says to.
Each chunk is hashed and compressed. A chunk the store already has is not written again.
Directories become pages of about sixty entries. A one file change rewrites one small page.
The new root is the commit. It goes into the store, and nothing old is touched.

left.title: Flat directories
items: The whole listing is written again
left.say: With flat directories, changing one file rewrites the whole listing.

right.title: Paged directories
items: Only one page is written again
right.say: With pages, only the page holding that file is written again.

scenes.label: of the toy's growth per late snapshot was directory structure
scenes.say: In my toy, structure was most of what each late snapshot cost. The file content was the smaller part.

scenes.text: Measure payload and structure separately. How you encode the tree can matter as much as how you deduplicate the files.
scenes.say: When you size a snapshot store, count payload and structure separately.
Chunk by content, store each chunk once, and page the tree.
